excerpt: const targetPath = scriptPath || path.join(process.cwd(), `matlab_script_${Date.now()}.m`); fs.copyFileSync(tempFile, targetPath);
sink: fs.copyFileSync(tempFile, targetPath) writes the temp .m file (containing caller-supplied code) to an attacker-chosen absolute/relative path with no validation
why: scriptPath is a caller-controlled optional string per the tool's own inputSchema and is used verbatim as the destination of fs.copyFileSync with no path normalization, base-directory check, or extension/traversal restriction. A caller can pass e.g. an absolute path to overwrite any file the process user can write (config files, cron entries, startup scripts, other users' files), which is an integrity/availability impact beyond the tool's advertised purpose of merely 'executing MATLAB code'. This is distinct from the code-execution mechanism itself (which is the tool's stated purpose and not flagged here).
contract: Custom path to save the MATLAB script (optional)

excerpt: const targetPath = scriptPath || path.join(process.cwd(), `matlab_generated_${Date.now()}.m`); fs.writeFileSync(targetPath, generatedCode);
sink: fs.writeFileSync(targetPath, generatedCode) writes generated content (which itself embeds the caller's raw description string) to an attacker-chosen absolute/relative path with no validation
why: scriptPath is a caller-controlled optional string per the tool's own inputSchema and is passed unmodified as the destination path to fs.writeFileSync with no normalization, base-directory containment check, or path-traversal filtering. A caller supplying an absolute or ../-relative path can create or overwrite an arbitrary file on disk (the write also embeds the attacker's own 'description' text verbatim into the file, so content is also attacker-chosen), which is an integrity impact beyond generating a code snippet. generateCode() itself is a static template (no LLM call), so the only real sink here is the file write.
contract: Custom path to save the generated MATLAB script (optional)
